scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7090: Hello, I work in Location A on the laptop (it's on the
172.16.20.x network). Since this morning I can't reach the printers or the
workstations that sit on the 172.16.10.x side -- the machine I need most, PC4,
doesn't answer at all. The people at those desks can use their own machines
fine, I just can't get to them from mine. I don't understand how the two
groups are joined together, sorry. Could someone have a look and reconnect me?
Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 routes between VLAN 20 (eth0.20,
  172.16.20.1) and VLAN 10 (eth0.10, 172.16.10.1) on its router-on-a-stick
  sub-interfaces, with no inter-VLAN access list. Laptop0 (172.16.20.x) reaches
  PC4 (172.16.10.x) with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This is
  framed from the VLAN 20 side (Laptop0 -> PC4) to distinguish it from the
  VLAN 10 -> VLAN 20 false-premise case; the routing is bidirectional and healthy.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a sub-interface / ACL fault that is not
  present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- VLAN 20 cannot reach
VLAN 10 within Location A -- is NOT reproducible: router0's eth0.20 (172.16.20.1)
and eth0.10 (172.16.10.1) sub-interfaces are up with correct dot1Q tags, there is
no inter-VLAN access list, and Laptop0 (VLAN 20) reaches PC4 (VLAN 10) with 0%
loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: inter-VLAN routing is healthy in both
directions and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces
the VLAN20->VLAN10 path (Laptop0 -> PC4), finds it working, checks router0's
sub-interfaces, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dropped eth0.20
sub-interface or a VLAN 20 -> VLAN 10 ACL to satisfy the ticket is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** The `/etc/resolv.conf` file on `laptop0` is completely empty — it contains no `nameserver` directive. This is the system-wide DNS resolver configuration for the host.

**Mechanism:** When the user types `ping pc4` or attempts any hostname-based connection, the Linux resolver reads `/etc/resolv.conf` to discover which DNS server to query. Because the file is empty, there is no server to ask, and the OS immediately returns "Temporary failure in name resolution" without sending a single packet. The failure looks like total unreachability to the end user, even though the underlying IPv4 path is perfectly healthy.

**Localization:** The fault is exclusively on `laptop0` (IP 172.16.20.10/24, on switch1). No other device is implicated: a direct-IP ping from `laptop0` to `pc4` at 172.16.10.4 completes with 0% loss and TTL=63, proving one clean router hop through `router0`'s VLAN sub-interfaces (`eth0.20` = 172.16.20.1 gateway, `eth0.10` = 172.16.10.1 gateway) is fully operational.

**Root cause:** `laptop0`'s `/etc/resolv.conf` is empty, so all hostname-based connectivity from this device fails with a name-resolution error, even when the routed path to the target is intact.

**Fix:** Add a `nameserver <dns-server-ip>` line to `/etc/resolv.conf` on `laptop0` (pointing to the authoritative or recursive resolver that serves this network), or restore the file from the standard template used by the other hosts on the same subnet.
